Strategic HR · Navigating Power

Same Fact, Different Filter

You already know how to build a strong case. Now you're learning something new: the same case can land in very different ways, depending on who is listening. The facts don't change. But the way each person hears them does. If you understand this in advance, you have real influence. If you don't, you're just relying on luck.

Before You Start · Who You're Coaching
Listen to the brief

As a strategic HR advisor, your job isn't only inside your own company. You work with client executives too: sitting in on interviews, hearing the politics nobody puts in writing, and flagging what could go wrong before it does. Renata is one of your clients, a director at Valore Bank who is learning to navigate exactly these situations. In parts of this lesson, you'll step directly into her shoes. That's a real coaching technique: it builds the same instinct you'll later use to guide her through the real thing.

Lead-In
Question 01

Why does the same piece of information often need to be explained differently to different people, even when nothing about the information itself changes?

Question 02

What is the difference between advising someone and simply telling them what they want to hear?

Question 03

When does timing matter more than the quality of an idea itself?

01The Filters

Every executive in the room filters the same information in a different way. Their role shapes what they reward and what they punish. If you understand their filter, you can predict their objection before they say it.

CEO
Chief Executive Officer
Asks first
"How does this move the story I'm telling the board?"
Fears
Being pego(a) de surpresaSer surpreendido por algo negativo que você não viu chegando, especialmente em público.Other ways to say this: caught off guard, taken by surprise in front of people he answers to
Tends to ignore
Small operational details, unless they would change the mensagem central / narrativa principalNão é "manchete de jornal" aqui, é usado de forma figurada para significar a ideia principal, a frase de uma linha que resume a história toda.Other ways to say this: the main message, the top-line story he's telling the board
CFO
Chief Financial Officer
Asks first
"Where does this show up on the numbers, and when?"
Fears
A number that surprises her later, after she's already dado a aprovação formalAprovar oficialmente algo, geralmente por escrito, assumindo responsabilidade por essa decisão.Other ways to say this: approved, greenlit, given the go-ahead
Tends to ignore
Good results that are hard to put into numbers
COO
Chief Operating Officer
Asks first
"Who executes this, and what breaks while they do?"
Fears
A plan that looks clean on a slide and falls apart on the floor
Tends to ignore
Strategic ideas with no clear delivery date
CRO
Chief Risk Officer
Asks first
"What's the exposição (ao risco)O grau em que a empresa está vulnerável a uma perda financeira ou reputacional caso algo dê errado.Other ways to say this: risk exposure, downside, potential loss if this goes wrong, and who owns that?"
Fears
Being the last to know about a risk that was already visible
Tends to ignore
Talk about benefits that ignores the risk first
CHRO
Chief Human Resources Officer
Asks first
"What does this do to the people who have to live with it?"
Fears
A decision that quietly damages retenção de talentosA capacidade da empresa de manter seus funcionários, especialmente os de alto desempenho, por mais tempo.Other ways to say this: keeping people, staff turnover (inverse) or trust
Tends to ignore
Financial pressure that ignores the impact on people
Think about it
The facts in a proposal stay the same. So why does the same proposal need a different opening line for each of these five people?
Model answer

Each role is judged by a different result, so each person is listening for a different signal first. If you open with that signal, you get past their filter before you even make your request.

R
Renatamessages you the morning after a budget meeting
"I don't get it. I opened with how this hire would help our long-term client relationships, and the CFO shut me down in two minutes. She didn't even let me finish the slide."
Your intervention
Solid moveThis goes straight at the filter. The CFO didn't reject the idea, she rejected being asked to trust a relationship story before seeing a number. Renata needs a different opening, not a longer one.
RiskyEscalating past the CFO without addressing why she said no can damage a relationship Renata will need again, and it still doesn't fix the real problem: the pitch didn't speak her language.
RiskyMore detail won't help if the CFO already stopped listening. The order of the pitch was the problem, not the amount of information in it.
02Sponsors & Timing

A good idea can die quietly if you present it at the wrong moment, with no support in the room. The idea itself is usually fine. The problem is the timing.

Walking In Cold

  • The room hears the idea for the first time
  • Objections vêm à tona / surgemAparecer ou se tornar visível, geralmente algo que estava escondido ou não havia sido dito antes.Other ways to say this: come up, emerge, come to light live, in front of everyone
  • You're defending and explaining at the same time
  • A single skeptic can travar / paralisarFazer algo parar de avançar ou progredir, geralmente de forma temporária mas frustrante.Other ways to say this: hold up, bring to a halt, freeze progress the whole room

Walking In With a Sponsor

  • Someone in the room has already seen it and backs it
  • Objections were raised and answered privately, beforehand
  • You're presenting a decision, not pitching a concept
  • A skeptic has to challenge two people, not one
Think about it
What does an internal sponsor actually change about a proposal, if the content of the proposal stays exactly the same?
Model answer

A sponsor changes the social risk of saying yes. Without a sponsor, you are the first person to take a position. With a sponsor, you are joining a position that already has support and credibility.

A Sponsor in Practice
Listen to the story

Renata wants the bank to add a new ponto de verificação antifraudeUma etapa extra no processo em que o sistema ou a equipe checa sinais de fraude antes de deixar o cliente avançar, como confirmar documentos ou identidade com mais cuidado.Other ways to say this: verification step, screening step, control point to the client onboarding process. It's a strong idea, but it will add two extra days to onboarding for every client, and Compliance has already proposed similar checks twice before without success.

Instead of taking it straight to the risk committee, she asks for fifteen minutes with the COO first. She explica passo a passoExplicar algo a alguém de forma clara e detalhada, geralmente passo a passo, para garantir que a pessoa entenda completamente.Other ways to say this: explain step by step, take someone through, break it down for the operational impact honestly, including the two extra days, and she comes ready for the question she knows he'll ask: "who executes this, and what breaks while they do?" By the end of the meeting, he tells her he's convinced.

Three days later, in the risk committee meeting, the COO speaks before Renata even finishes her introduction. He says he's already reviewed the plan and the operational side is solid. Two people raise small questions. Nobody blocks it.

Renata didn't just have a good idea. She spent fifteen minutes preparing the one person whose filter mattered most in that room, before the room ever saw the idea.

Think about it
What did Renata actually do in her private meeting with the COO, beyond simply describing her idea?
Model answer

She prepared for his specific filter before he ever asked about it in the room. That's why his support came so fast, and why he was willing to speak for the plan in front of everyone else.

Reading the Timing

The same proposal can seem too early in January and obvious in March, even though nothing in the proposal itself changed. What changed is the ciclo orçamentárioO período recorrente (geralmente anual) em que uma empresa planeja, aprova e revisa seus gastos.Other ways to say this: fiscal cycle, planning cycle, a recent problem that made the risk clear, or a competitor's move that made waiting more costly. Timing isn't luck. It's something you can watch and plan for.

Think about it
What signs tell you this is the wrong moment for a proposal, even when the proposal itself is good?
Model answer

Signs include a budget cycle that has already closed, a decision-maker who is dealing with an unrelated crisis, or a recent failure in a similar project that people haven't processed yet. Any of these can kill a good idea for reasons that have nothing to do with its quality.

R
Renatamessages you two days before she presents to the risk committee
"I've got the proposal ready. Slides are done, numbers check out. I go in front of the committee on Thursday."
Your intervention
Solid moveThis is the real question. A ready deck without a sponsor still walks in cold. Fifteen minutes with the right person before Thursday can change how the whole room reacts.
RiskyA polished deck doesn't replace someone in the room already backing her. This misses the actual risk in the situation.
RiskyCovering every objection in advance doesn't change the social dynamic in the room, and it can even make Renata look like she's defending the idea alone.
03The Language

Eight expressions that native speakers use to talk about power, alliances, and self-protection at work. Hover over the highlighted phrase to see the translation. Then make your choice.

1

The new reporting system will save hours every week. But three directors will need to change how their teams work. Before the proposal goes to the comitê diretorGrupo de líderes que se reúne regularmente para aprovar e acompanhar as decisões mais importantes de um projeto.Other ways to say this: leadership committee, oversight committee, the project lead spends two weeks meeting each director alone. He listens to their concerns and adjusts the plan. By the time the committee meets, all three directors already support the idea. He spent those two weeks working to conseguir apoio/adesãoConquistar o apoio genuíno de pessoas-chave antes de uma decisão formal, para que elas cheguem já favoráveis.Other ways to say this: build support, bring people on board, win people over.

Think about it
Why is getting buy-in before a formal meeting more effective than presenting a finished plan and asking for approval right away?
Model answer

In private conversations, people can raise concerns without losing face in front of their peers. This lets the presenter adjust the plan before it becomes public. So the formal meeting becomes a confirmation, not a negotiation.

Your call, as the project lead
Solid moveIf you win over the hardest critic first, you remove the objection most likely to disrupt the room. That critic often becomes an unexpected advocate.
RiskyPresenting a finished plan without warning invites public objections. These are harder to resolve live than they would have been in private.
RiskyBuy-in from people who already agree with you doesn't remove the resistance that's still in the room.
2

Renata walks into a budget meeting ready to make her case for a new hire. Within thirty seconds, she notices the CFO's arms are crossed and he keeps glancing at his phone, while the COO is nodding along to whatever the last speaker said. She quietly shortens her pitch and leads with the cost-saving angle instead of the growth angle. Renata is good at ler o ambiente/a salaPerceber rapidamente o clima, o humor e as reações das pessoas presentes para ajustar sua abordagem em tempo real.Other ways to say this: gauge the mood, sense the atmosphere, pick up on the vibe.

Think about it
What is the difference between reading the room and simply changing your opinion to please whoever is listening?
Model answer

Reading the room changes how you present an argument, and in what order. It doesn't change what the argument actually is. Changing your opinion just to please the room means changing your actual message, and over time this damages your credibility.

Step into her shoes: your call, as Renata
Solid moveIf you lead with the point most likely to land, you keep your message the same, and you give your argument its best chance of being heard.
RiskyDelivering a rehearsed pitch, no matter the room's mood, ignores real signals about what will actually persuade this specific audience today.
RiskyGiving up completely at the first sign of resistance means losing ground you could have won with a small change in your approach.
3

The compliance director is pushing hard for a new approval process. This process will slow down every mesa de operaçõesA equipe que estrutura e executa transações financeiras, como negociações de crédito ou fusões.Other ways to say this: trading desk, transaction team in the bank. Nobody says this out loud, but she was the one who approved the process that failed last quarter, and her name is now attached to the fix. She isn't just protecting the bank. She also tem interesse pessoal no resultadoTer algo pessoal em risco (reputação, carreira, recursos) no resultado de uma decisão, o que motiva o engajamento além do dever profissional.Other ways to say this: have a personal stake, be personally invested, have something on the line.

Think about it
Why is it useful to know who has personal skin in the game, even when their stated reason is completely valid?
Model answer

Knowing someone's personal stake doesn't make their argument wrong. But it explains why they feel so strongly, and it helps you predict where they won't compromise, which helps you negotiate the parts that really can be negotiated.

Your call, as an outside observer
Solid moveIf you separate the value of the proposal from the motive behind it, you can judge both honestly. Neither one affects the other.
RiskyRejecting a proposal just because the person pushing it benefits personally ignores the fact that the proposal might still be right.
RiskyAutomatically supporting something just because someone has a personal stake in it replaces judgment with sympathy.
4

The launch date is delayed and the client is furious. In the reunião de retrospectivaReunião realizada após o fim (ou falha) de um projeto para analisar o que aconteceu e por quê.Other ways to say this: review meeting, retrospective, the project lead says the delay was "entirely due to a scheduling error by the operations team," without mentioning the three change requests he approved late. Operations has no chance to respond before the client hears that version. Everyone in the room can see that he chose to jogar alguém debaixo do ônibusCulpar publicamente outra pessoa ou equipe por um problema, para se proteger, mesmo que a culpa seja compartilhada ou injusta.Other ways to say this: scapegoat someone, pin the blame on, shift the blame.

Think about it
What is the long-term cost of throwing a colleague under the bus, even when it protects you in that specific meeting?
Model answer

It protects your reputation once, but it also teaches everyone watching that you'll do it again. This makes people reluctant to collaborate with you or share information openly in the future.

Your call, in the same meeting
Solid moveOwning your part of the timeline alongside the real cause keeps the account accurate and protects your credibility for the next project.
RiskyStaying silent while a colleague takes the blame protects your position today, but it costs you trust later.
RiskyDefending someone else without acknowledging your own role feels performative, and the real cause still isn't addressed.
5

Before presenting the new pricing model, the analyst checks it with legal, reviews three prior client complaints, and prepares a one-page answer to the question she knows the CFO always asks about margem (de lucro)A diferença entre o preço de venda e o custo de algo, expressa geralmente como porcentagem.Other ways to say this: profit margin, markup. Colleagues tease her for over-preparing. She says she'd rather spend an extra hour now than get caught without an answer later. She's simply learning to se precaver / cobrir todos os ângulosSe preparar com antecedência para as objeções ou perguntas mais prováveis, reduzindo o risco de ser pega de surpresa.Other ways to say this: do your homework, anticipate objections, leave no stone unturned.

Think about it
At what point does covering your bases stop being good preparation and start being too much caution?
Model answer

It becomes excessive when the preparation tries to avoid any possible criticism, instead of addressing the objections that are actually likely. This slows decisions down without really reducing risk.

Your call, watching this pattern repeat
Solid moveUnderstanding what she's actually preparing for tells you the difference between sharp anticipation and anxious over-preparation, and whether the habit is worth encouraging.
RiskyPushing her to move faster without knowing what the extra hour actually protects against risks cutting real preparation, not just excess.
RiskyReading preparation as a lack of confidence confuses two very different things: not trusting your numbers, and knowing exactly which question is coming.
6

The VP of Operations has never once said a bad word about the new client portal in a meeting. But in every steering committee, right before a vote, he's the one who says, "I've seen this work, and I think it's worth the investment," which tends to settle the room. Nobody assigned him that role. He just became the project's padrinho/defensor internoPessoa influente que defende ativamente uma iniciativa dentro da organização, emprestando sua credibilidade a ela.Other ways to say this: internal advocate, sponsor, backer.

Think about it
What does a project gain from having an informal champion that it doesn't gain from having formal approval alone?
Model answer

Formal approval says a project is allowed to move forward. A champion actively lends personal credibility to it in the room, which reassures people who are still undecided and don't want to bet on an idea alone.

Your call, as the project lead
Solid moveA champion's support depends on staying informed enough to keep vouching for the project. Keeping him in the loop protects the asset you've already built.
RiskyAssuming silent support lasts forever ignores that his credibility depends on staying current, and it fades if he's left out of updates.
RiskyHanding over formal leadership solves a problem that didn't exist, and gives up ownership you didn't need to give up.
7

Everyone in the risk committee agrees the sistema legadoUm sistema de tecnologia antigo, ainda em uso, que a empresa não substituiu apesar de já estar ultrapassado.Other ways to say this: outdated system, old infrastructure needs to be replaced. Every quarter, someone proposes a small patch instead, "just to get through this reporting cycle without disruption." Three years and eleven patches later, the same conversation happens again. The committee keeps choosing to empurrar com a barriga / adiar o problemaAdiar repetidamente uma decisão difícil, aplicando soluções paliativas em vez de resolver a causa raiz.Other ways to say this: put off the decision, delay the inevitable, punt on the issue.

Think about it
Why might a group of experienced executives repeatedly choose a short-term patch over a decision they all agree is necessary?
Model answer

The cost of the real decision is immediate and falls on whoever approves it, while the cost of delay is spread out across future quarters. So it feels rational to delay, even though it's expensive for the company as a whole.

Your call, presenting to the committee this quarter
Solid moveMaking the cost of delay visible and immediate, in language the committee already uses, removes the incentive that's been driving the pattern for three years.
RiskyContinuing the pattern confirms it's still the easiest path to take, and guarantees the same conversation returns next quarter.
RiskyNaming the pattern publicly can put people on the defensive, without giving them a new, less costly option to choose instead.
8

During a heated negotiation over shared quadro de funcionáriosO número de pessoas empregadas em uma equipe ou departamento.Other ways to say this: staff numbers, workforce, the director sends an email copying the CEO, stating publicly that the other department "refused to cooperate at every step." It isn't true, and everyone who was in the actual conversations knows it. The other director says nothing back, but from that day on, no one on his team shares information with that department again. In one email, the first director managed to queimar uma ponteDestruir permanentemente uma relação ou aliança, geralmente por um ato de curto prazo que traz ganho imediato mas fecha portas futuras.Other ways to say this: damage a relationship beyond repair, sever ties, torch a relationship.

Think about it
Why can a single public move like this cost more than it appears to save in the moment?
Model answer

The email might win the immediate argument, but it destroys future cooperation, information-sharing, and goodwill. Over time, that could have been worth far more than whatever was gained in that one exchange.

Your call, as the director on the receiving end
Solid moveCorrecting the record privately protects the facts without turning it into a second public spectacle that would cost both departments even more.
RiskyEscalating publicly in return matches the original move's damage and turns a one-sided burned bridge into a mutual one.
RiskyWithdrawing silently lets the false version stand uncorrected, and it quietly damages collaboration for both teams going forward.
R
Renatamessages you late at night, clearly upset
"A colleague just sent an email to the whole steering committee saying I dropped the ball on my part of the project. It's not true, and I want to reply-all with the real timeline right now."
Your intervention
Solid moveThis protects the facts without turning it into a second public fight, and it's a much easier conversation once the anger from tonight has cooled down.
RiskyMatching the public move in public escalates the damage for both people, and it rarely reads as calm when it's sent late at night, upset.
RiskyLetting a false version stand uncorrected quietly damages her credibility and future collaboration with that team.

05Your Reality

None of this is about manipulation. It's about presenting the same truth in a way the person in front of you can actually hear and act on.

Discussion 01

What is the difference between adapting your message to a stakeholder's filter and simply telling each person what they want to hear?

Model answer

Adapting the message means changing the framing and the order of information, while keeping the substance the same for everyone. Telling people what they want to hear means changing the message itself, which corrói a confiançaDesgastar a confiança de alguém aos poucos, de forma quase imperceptível, até que ela desapareça.Other ways to say this: undermine trust, wear down trust once it's discovered.

Discussion 02

Why does having an internal sponsor change how a decision-maker evaluates risk, even when the proposal itself hasn't changed?

Model answer

A sponsor transfers some of their own credibility onto the proposal, which lowers the perceived risk of supporting it. The decision-maker is no longer the only one whose judgment is on the line.

Discussion 03

What separates building genuine alliances from simply collecting favors to cobrar (um favor)Pedir de volta um favor que alguém te deve, cobrando o retorno de algo que você fez por essa pessoa antes.Other ways to say this: cash in a favor, collect on a favor later?

Model answer

Genuine alliances are built on mutual value that holds up even when nothing is being asked for. Collecting favors only exists to be cashed in later, and people tend to sense that and resent it over time.

Discussion 04

How does timing change the fate of an identical proposal presented three months apart?

Model answer

The proposal doesn't change, but the context around it does. Budget availability, recent problems, and competing priorities shift the room's apetite / disposiçãoO quanto uma pessoa ou organização está disposta a aceitar risco, custo ou mudança em um determinado momento.Other ways to say this: tolerance, willingness, readiness for a new commitment. That can turn the same idea from too early to overdue.

Internal Process Note · Client Onboarding

A Fraud-Detection Checkpoint, Step by Step

This is what actually happens inside the onboarding flow, and exactly where Renata's proposal changes it.

Already in place
Renata's addition
1
Document Upload Already in place

The client submits an ID document and a proof of address online, as part of the normal onboarding form.

2
Automatic Screening Already in place

The system checks the documents against government listas de restriçãoListas oficiais de pessoas ou empresas proibidas de fazer negócios, por sanções, suspeita de crime financeiro, ou outros motivos legais.Other ways to say this: sanctions lists, restricted-party lists, blacklists and looks for signs that a file was edited or faked. Most clients pass this step in minutes.

3
A Red Flag Pauses the Process Renata's addition

If something looks off, like an address that doesn't match, a name close to one on a watchlist, or a document that looks altered, the process now stops the automatic approval and sends the case to a person instead. Today, flagged cases still go through automatically.

4
Manual Review Renata's addition

A compliance analyst checks the flagged case by hand, and may ask the client for one more document to confirm their identity. This role and step don't exist in the current process.

5
Final Decision Already in place

Only after this step clears does the account become fully active. The approval step already exists, but under the new process, flagged cases reach it later, after a human has looked at them.

This is the real trade-off Renata is asking the bank to accept. Most clients still pass in minutes, but the small number the process flags now go through steps 3 and 4, which don't exist today. That's exactly where the two extra days in the story come from.
